text: Eighty minutes, a man with no name, and a taxi ride that behaves less like transport than like a verdict. Bang Bang runs its anonymous city dweller through one absurdity after another — a gang more baffling than menacing, gunfire used as punctuation — and never stops to account for any of it. The furniture is crime-film furniture: the chase, the holdup, the standoff. All of it comes apart in the handling. What keeps the thing upright is rhythm rather than plot, and a conviction that the people onscreen are animals wearing city clothes. Andrea Tonacci works at a length that forces compression; nothing is developed, everything is delivered. Abraccine's list of a hundred Brazilian films later found room for it, which is a strange fate for a picture this uninterested in behaving.

A daughter who was four years old in 1977 sets out to reconstruct parents she cannot properly remember, and finds that memory will not hold still long enough. Albertina Carri's parents were disappeared by Argentina's military junta, and Los rubios refuses the shape that sentence usually imposes. It is not testimony. She was four when it happened, which sets a hard limit on what can honestly be claimed as recall. Fantasy therefore sits beside recollection without being ranked below it; invention is handled as part of the evidence rather than as a failure of it, which is a difficult position to hold for eighty-nine minutes, and it is held. The making of the film stays visible throughout — the arranging, the second-guessing, the accounts that will not fit together. What the film will not do is settle, and that refusal is the argument it is making.

A company hands out the title of model worker at a party, and the man later hunted for what happened there had nothing to do with the factory at all. Deraldo sells his own verse in São Paulo, printed cheap and moved by hand, a poet from the Northeast making a living out of pamphlets in a city with no particular use for them. The mistaken identity is not a comic device but an administrative one: an employer's paperwork decides who he is, gets it wrong, and cannot be argued with. João Batista de Andrade films the migrant's São Paulo as a place of counters and queues and documents, where the standing question is what a man can prove. Ninety-seven minutes is long enough to watch someone's own name stop working for him.

Ângela Carne e Osso — the surname translates as Meat and Bone — moves through a circle of small-time criminals who cannot look away from her. All the wanting in the film is done by the men; she supplies the gravity and they arrange themselves around it, which turns their delinquency into something closer to courtship and considerably less flattering. Rogério Sganzerla runs comedy, fantasy and melodrama at once rather than in sequence, so a gag can turn cruel inside a single shot and the cruelty can collapse back into farce. Ninety-three minutes, made in Brazil in 1969, with a tone that will not settle into satire or into sympathy. Sex is treated here as a form of authority, and the men who submit to it are the actual subject.

A foreman comes down to Posadas to hire men for a yerba mate plantation, and the hiring is the last orderly transaction in the film. The year inside the story is 1915. Köhner rules his stretch of the north by force and takes no trouble to disguise it, while the doctor traveling with him, and the doctor's daughter, arrive carrying the assumption that an agreement means something. Mario Soffici gives the plantation its own weather: heat, hours, and a distance from any authority that could be appealed to. Eighty-seven minutes, most of them spent watching that distance do the work of a fence. Nothing about the place is exotic to the men inside it; the plantation is where the work was, and where they now are. The Museo del Cine's Argentine survey keeps it in the record.

Children run alongside a moving train with their hands out, shouting for coins, and the film is barely longer than the crossing itself. Thirty-three minutes, the city of Santa Fe, 1960. The neighbourhood is known as Tire Dié after that shout — toss me a dime — and Fernando Birri turns the shout into a method: go to the place, count what is there, let the people who live there say it. It was built as a survey on film, the first such in Latin America by the reckoning that followed, and the arithmetic is audible in it. That runtime is not a short version of something longer; it is the length the subject takes. Nothing is arranged for pity. The children are quick, practised, and running a route they know far better than any passenger leaning out of a window above them.

Comedy sometimes needs nothing more than a room, a set of regulars, and enough hours for them to repeat themselves. Bar Esperança gives itself a bar in Ipanema and a hundred and nineteen minutes, and the plot mostly arrives through the door with whoever comes in next. Hugo Carvana shot it in Rio de Janeiro in 1983. The setting carries the structure: a neighbourhood bar is one of the few places where people with nothing in common can plausibly end up in the same conversation, and where a romance can start, stall and restart without anyone having to travel. The regulars are eccentrics, and the film neither tidies them up nor explains them. Two hours held together by company rather than incident is harder to bring off than it sounds.

A rich man buries his young wife and then meets a woman with her face. Beyond Oblivion refuses to make a ghost story of that; what it follows is the question of what Fernando de Arellano, newly bereaved and unused to being refused, will ask of a living woman who happens to resemble the dead one. Mónica is the one being asked. The three genres attached to the film — drama, romance, thriller — are not alternating modes but one situation described from different sides of the room, and which of them is playing at any moment depends on whose position the camera has taken. Hugo del Carril made it in Argentina in 1956, ninety-two minutes, in a register where devotion and possession are hard to tell apart and the difficulty is the whole design.

The doctor is a houseguest, which is the only reason he is ever in a room with the daughter of the house at all. Nineteenth-century Brazil, a house in the country where a visiting physician is an event in itself, and a courtship conducted under supervision or in the small gaps between other people's attentions. He is there to treat her, which gives the arrangement its cover. Walter Lima Jr. takes a hundred and eighteen minutes over it, and the length is the argument: the period's machinery — who may speak to whom, for how long, with which door open — is the plot rather than its decor. The father's disapproval is not a late complication but the condition under which every scene operates. The seduction is less an event than an accumulation of permitted minutes, and the film counts them one by one.

The conspiracy is the work of intellectuals and rich men, which is the first thing wrong with it. Joaquim Pedro de Andrade spends seventy-eight minutes on a failed independence plot in colonial Brazil and declines to inflate any of it into pageant; the scale stays small, the talk stays close. He films history as deliberation rather than as event — the thing is discussed long before it is anything else. History has already published the outcome, so suspense is neither available nor attempted. What gets examined instead is the gap between what these men said to one another in private and what any of them proved willing to do about it. Made in Brazil in 1972, and nothing in it is nostalgic. It sits on Abraccine's hundred-title survey of Brazilian cinema, though the film itself takes a dim view of monuments.

A man leaves everything behind for a paradise he first saw in a tourist agency. Carlos Reichenbach hangs a Faust on that: the heir to a bankrupt cigarette factory, out of money and out of explanations, following an agency's picture toward self-knowledge with a Mephistophelean figure at his elbow supplying encouragement. The bargain on offer in 1986 Brazil is not for a soul but for a destination, and the film is candid that somebody manufactured the destination and priced it. That image is the most honest thing here; it promises exactly what it was produced to promise. Ninety minutes, tipped hard into fantasy, unembarrassed by the literary source and unwilling to treat it with deference. Cigarettes, bankruptcy, package tourism — three things the picture keeps circling, and it disguises none of them as metaphor.

Something falls out of the sky in 1959 and lands in a hen coop. It may be the Russian satellite; the man who owns the hens is in no position to determine that, and everyone with an interest in the answer is glad to determine it for him. Carlos Manga gets ninety-eight minutes of comedy out of that imbalance, and the joke holds because it is structural rather than topical: the largest contest on the planet touches down on the smallest property in Brazil, and the owner of the property is the last person consulted. The space age enters as gossip rather than as technology; nobody onscreen needs to understand a satellite to want one. The satire runs on hierarchy more than on politics. It is broad, played fast, and quite certain that the person to be laughed at is not the farmer.

The plot is a home renovation — walls down, dust in everything, strangers in the kitchen from morning to night. Arnaldo Jabor keeps a middle-class family and the men it has hired inside the same apartment for most of a hundred and eleven minutes, and the flat gets smaller by the reel. This is class comedy conducted at a range of one metre, and it sours on schedule: there is nowhere to be private about one's opinions, and the noise makes the pretence of an ordinary life ridiculous. Then stranger things start happening in the apartment, and the film neither explains them nor changes register. Brazil, 1978. A domestic inconvenience is given the seriousness of an infestation, and the household's insistence that everything is manageable is the funniest thing in it.

The Tietê runs through São Paulo, and the whole of The Margin takes place within a few metres of its banks. The people there are the ones the city has stopped counting: women who sell themselves, the man who takes their earnings, a man who cannot look after himself. Ozualdo Ribeiro Candeias does not organise them into a story so much as into a stretch of riverbank where the same day keeps arriving. Something like a romance forms anyway, in conditions that give it nowhere to go, and the film is unsentimental about that arithmetic. What it has in place of plot is texture: water, refuse, the noise of a city carrying on somewhere above. Made in Brazil in 1967, ninety-six minutes, and hard going. It is not, however, indifferent, and Candeias keeps those two apart.
